property_summary: After any Deposit by an address, the contract's balances mapping for that depositor equals the previous balance plus the deposited msg.value (i.e., Deposit accumulates balances); the mutant overwrites instead and thus can make balances(addr) != old + value for some inputs.

For any depositor address a and any nonzero deposit v (within 0..type(uint256).max), after calling Deposit() from a with value v the reference preserves that balances(a) is at least v (i.e., the depositor's recorded balance is not less than the single deposit amount); the mutant can overwrite and make balances(a) < v for some inputs, so this invariant distinguishes them.

For any two distinct actors a and b and any nonzero deposit v by a after b previously deposited w, the reference preserves b's recorded balance (balances(b) remains equal to its prior value) — the mutant can corrupt a different key's balance (overwriting balances[msg.sender] = msg.value may, due to storage collision in some contexts or mistaken implementation, cause balances of other addresses to change) and thus can make balances(b) differ from its prior value.

For any depositor a and any two sequential deposits v1 then v2 by the same a, the reference preserves that balances(a) after the second deposit equals the sum of the prior balance plus v2 (i.e., Deposit accumulates so the increment from the second deposit equals v2); the mutant that overwrites balance with msg.value breaks this when v1 != 0 because the second deposit will leave balances(a)==v2 instead of prior+v2.

For every depositor a and any initial setup where some other address b made a prior deposit of nonzero amount, a deposit by a must not change b's stored balance (the reference never alters other accounts' balances; the mutant can, for some inputs, cause another address's stored balance to change), so balances(b) after a's Deposit equals its prior value.

For any caller and deposit amount, the reference contract increases the caller's stored balance by exactly the deposited msg.value; the mutant sometimes increases it by 2*msg.value, violating that equality.

For any depositor address A and nonzero deposit amount v, after calling Deposit() the reference contract's balances(A) increases by exactly v (i.e. balances(A)_after - balances(A)_before == v); the mutant that double-credits breaks this by sometimes increasing by 2*v.

For any depositor address A and deposit amount v, calling Deposit() increases C.balances(A) by exactly v; the mutant that double-credits sometimes increases balances(A) by 2*v, violating this equality.

For any caller A and deposit value v, the total sum of all stored balances in the contract increases by exactly v after A calls Deposit(); the mutant that double-credits the depositor causes the total stored-sum to sometimes increase by 2*v, breaking this invariant.

For any depositor A and deposit amount v where v>0 and A is a contract that accepts Ether, the reference increases A's stored balance by exactly v (so balances(A)_after - balances(A)_before == v); the mutant that double-credits will make this difference equal 2*v for some inputs (a contract depositor), so the property distinguishes them.

For any sender and any msg.value >= 0, calling Deposit credits the sender's balances entry by exactly the full msg.value; the mutant that only credits msg.value/2 violates this because some inputs (odd or even values) produce balances less than expected.

For any actor and any deposit amount, calling Deposit increases that actor's public balances entry by exactly the sent msg.value (the mutant credits only msg.value/2, so for some amounts balances differ).

For any depositor address and any nonzero even deposit amount, calling Deposit increases that depositor's public balances by exactly the sent msg.value; the mutant that credits only msg.value/2 breaks this (some even amounts still show a difference vs original if mutant halves), so the test uses an admissible domain (nonzero even amounts) that the reference always satisfies but the mutant fails for some inputs.

For any actor and any nonzero deposit amount, after calling Deposit the contract's public balances for that actor increases by exactly the deposited msg.value (the mutant that credits only msg.value/2 can leave balances smaller for some fuzzed amounts).

For any depositor and any nonzero msg.value that is an odd number, after calling Deposit the reference C increases the depositor's public balances by exactly msg.value, whereas the mutant (which only credits msg.value/2) will sometimes make balances strictly less; the test constrains to odd, nonzero values so reference always adds full value while mutant can be detected.

After Deposit completes, every depositor's recorded balance equals the sum of their prior balance plus the deposited value (i.e., Deposit always updates balances before any external logging can observe old balances); the mutant that logs before updating allows a reentrant/malicious Log contract to observe and exploit the old balance causing c.balances(k) to differ for some key k.

For any caller and deposit amount, after calling Deposit through a malicious Log contract that re-enters, the contract's recorded balance for the depositor equals prior balance plus the deposited amount (reference updates balance before attacker observation); the mutant that logs before updating allows a reentrant Log to observe and disrupt the balance so this property can be violated.

For any depositor and any deposit amount, if the contract's configured Log is a reentrant attacker, then after Deposit completes the depositor's recorded balance equals its prior balance plus the deposited amount; the mutant that logs before updating allows the attacker to reenter and cause balances to differ.

For every depositor and deposit amount, when the contract's Log is a reentrant attacker that calls back into Deposit, the reference implementation always increases the depositor's recorded balance by the deposited amount (no attacker-visible intermediate state), whereas the mutant that logs before updating allows reentrant calls to observe and change balances so some key's balance can differ after Deposit.

For any depositor and deposit amount when the contract's Log is a malicious reentrant contract that calls back into Deposit, after Deposit completes the total sum of all recorded balances in C equals the total Ether actually held by C (i.e., balances sum == address(c).balance); the mutant that logs before updating allows reentrant manipulation during the logging call so this invariant can be violated for some inputs.

For any caller and any deposit value, calling Deposit increases that caller's balances[msg.sender] by exactly msg.value (i.e., balances after Deposit equals previous balance plus msg.value); the mutant removing the explicit overflow check can cause balances to differ (wrap) for some fuzzed inputs and attacker-controlled address.

For every depositor and deposit amount, the correct contract preserves the invariant that after calling Deposit the stored balances for any address equals its prior balance plus the deposited amount (no unexpected wrapping or change to other accounts); removing the explicit overflow check can break this under adversarially chosen prior balances and deposit amounts, making balances differ.

For every depositor and deposit amount, invoking Deposit preserves that the balances mapping at any address either remains unchanged for non-targeted addresses and increases for the caller by exactly the sent value in the reference; the mutant (removing the overflow check) can cause balances to wrap/change unexpectedly for some fuzzed prior balance and amount, so there exists inputs where balances(key) differs after Deposit between reference and mutant.

For any depositor and deposit amount where the depositor's prior balance plus the deposit does not overflow uint256, Deposit always succeeds and increases that depositor's balances by exactly the deposit; removing the explicit overflow check allows an input (prior balance and amount) that causes wrap/overflow behavior and thus breaks this property.

For any depositor and deposit amount where the depositor's prior balance is strictly less than 2**256 - amount, Deposit never reverts and afterwards the depositor's balances equals the prior balance plus amount; removing the explicit overflow check can allow inputs where addition wraps (or causes a revert in reference) and thus the mutant's behavior differs — the test constrains inputs so the reference always succeeds and then detects when balances differ between runs (manifesting for some fuzz input on the mutant).

For any uint input _val, the reference contract C allows SetMinSum(_val) to set MinSum to that exact value (unless Initialized prevented it), whereas the mutant rejects and reverts whenever _val < 1 ether, so there exist fuzzed _val values that make the mutant fail while the reference succeeds.

If the contract is not yet initialized, calling SetLogFile(x) must only succeed without changing Log when the call reverts due to initialized=true; the mutant assigns Log before checking initialized, so for some inputs (initialized=true) the reference reverts without changing Log while the mutant changes Log despite revert attempt.

For any address X, calling SetLogFile(X) when the contract is already initialized must not change the stored Log (the call reverts and Log stays as before); the mutant assigns Log before the initialized-check so for some X the Log value changes despite the call reverting.

For any address arg, calling SetLogFile(addr) on an already-initialized contract must not change the stored Log (the call reverts and leaves Log unchanged); the mutant assigns Log before the initialized-check so some calls with initialized=true will observe Log changed despite the call reverting.

If the contract is already initialized, calling SetLogFile(x) must never change the stored Log value (call either reverts or leaves Log unchanged); the mutant assigns Log before the initialized check so for some fuzzed _log addresses the stored Log in the mutant changes despite the call reverting, violating this invariant.

If the contract is already initialized, calling SetLogFile(...) must revert and must not change the stored Log pointer; the mutant assigns Log before checking initialized so for some _log addresses the mutant will change Log despite the call reverting.

For any non-zero address passed to SetLogFile, the reference contract stores that address in its Log state (so the public getter Log() returns the same non-zero address), whereas the mutant always sets Log to address(0) and thus violates this for many non-zero inputs.

For any non-zero address passed to SetLogFile, the correct contract records that exact address in its Log getter; the mutant instead stores address(0) so for some non-zero inputs the stored Log differs.

For every non-zero helper contract address provided to SetLogFile, the reference C stores that exact address in its public Log getter; the mutant instead stores address(0), so there exist non-zero addresses for which the stored Log differs.

For any non-zero address passed to SetLogFile, the reference C stores that exact address in its public Log getter; the mutant instead stores address(0) for all inputs, so there exist non-zero addresses where the stored Log differs.

For every non-zero address helper deployed and passed into SetLogFile, the reference C will allow SetLogFile to accept that address (i.e. calling SetLogFile with that address does not revert and the contract's state accepts a non-zero Log pointer), whereas the mutant silently replaces any passed-in address with address(0) causing the stored Log to be zero for some non-zero inputs — we assert that calling SetLogFile with a deployed helper address succeeds (does not revert) and leaves Log() non-zero.

After any Deposit() by an account sending a nonzero msg.value, the contract's stored balances[account] increases by msg.value from its previous value (i.e. new balance == old balance + msg.value); the mutant that assigns balances[msg.sender] = msg.value breaks this for inputs where the sender already had a nonzero balance.

For any caller and amount, after calling Deposit with msg.value = v, the contract's stored balances[caller] is at least the max(previous balance, v) (i.e., it never decreases below either the previous balance or the deposited amount); the mutant that sets balances[msg.sender] = msg.value can decrease a previously larger balance to v and thus violates this rule for callers with prior nonzero balances and smaller new deposits.

For any caller and deposit amount, after Deposit completes the caller's stored balance equals previous_balance + msg.value (i.e., Deposit always adds the incoming value to the existing balance); the mutant that does balances[msg.sender] = msg.value breaks this when the caller already has a nonzero previous balance and deposits a smaller amount.

For any caller and deposit amount, if the caller makes two deposits in sequence, the second deposit increases their stored balance by exactly the second deposit amount (i.e., balance_after_second == balance_after_first + second_amount); the mutant that overwrites balances instead of adding will violate this when the second deposit is to a caller who already has a nonzero balance.

For any caller and two sequential deposits v1 then v2 (both >0), the reference ensures final balance equals initial + v1 + v2 (i.e., Deposit is additive across successive deposits), while the mutant that assigns balances[msg.sender]=msg.value can reset the balance on the second deposit and thus violate this.

For any sender and any nonzero ETH value they send, calling Deposit succeeds and increases the contract's recorded balances[msg.sender] by the sent value (so address(c).balance grows accordingly); the mutant always reverts on Deposit (require(false)) and thus breaks this property for some inputs (e.g., any positive value).

For any caller and any nonzero ether amount, calling Deposit succeeds (does not revert) and increases both the contract balance and balances[caller] by the sent amount; the mutant with require(false) will cause Deposit to revert (fail) for some inputs, violating this rule.
